questions.prompt: Which principle says testing can show that defects are present but cannot prove they are absent?
options: Testing shows the presence, not the absence of defects
Exhaustive testing is impossible
Defects cluster together
Tests wear out
questions.explanation: This is principle one in CTFL v4.0. The others are separate principles about combinations, clustering and repetition.

questions.prompt: In CTFL v4.0, the pesticide paradox principle is now named...
options: Tests wear out
Absence-of-defects fallacy
Early testing saves time and money
Testing is context dependent
questions.explanation: CTFL v4.0 renamed it "tests wear out": repeating the same tests becomes less effective at finding new defects. The others are different principles.

questions.prompt: "Testing is context dependent" means the right test approach for a banking app may differ from that for a mobile game.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Risk, regulation, technology and life cycle all change how testing should be done; there is no single approach for all contexts.

questions.prompt: A login form has 3 fields, each accepting 100 different characters and up to 20 characters long. Why can't you test all inputs?
options: The number of combinations is astronomically large, so exhaustive testing is impossible; use techniques and prioritisation
Login forms cannot be tested
All inputs can be tested in a day with automation
Only valid inputs matter
questions.explanation: Exhaustive testing is impossible except in trivial cases, so testers use techniques, risk analysis and prioritisation. Automation does not make astronomical numbers feasible, and invalid inputs matter.

questions.prompt: Analysis shows 80% of defects in the last three releases were found in the payment and import modules. Which principle is this, and what does it suggest?
options: Defects cluster together; focus additional testing on those modules
Tests wear out; delete old tests
Early testing; start sooner
Absence-of-defects fallacy; stop testing
questions.explanation: Defect clustering (often a Pareto-like distribution) suggests targeting effort where defects concentrate. The other options apply other principles in ways that do not follow from the data.

questions.prompt: Which actions counter the "tests wear out" effect? Select all that apply.
options: Reviewing and updating tests regularly
Adding new tests and data variations
Using exploratory sessions in changed areas
Running the same tests more often
questions.explanation: Updating, adding variation and exploring keep tests finding new defects. Repeating the same tests more often makes the wear-out effect worse, though they still have regression value.

questions.prompt: A system passes all tests, has almost no open defects, yet users reject it because it does not fit their workflow. Which principle applies?
options: Absence-of-defects fallacy
Defects cluster together
Exhaustive testing is impossible
Tests wear out
questions.explanation: Finding and fixing many defects does not guarantee a successful system; it must also meet user needs, which calls for validation. The others do not explain the rejection.

questions.prompt: A team skips reviews and starts testing only after coding is complete. Late-found requirement defects cause a three-week delay. Which principle best explains the cost, and what should change?
options: Early testing saves time and money; review requirements and designs and start test analysis as early as possible
Testing is context dependent; change the context
Defects cluster together; only test requirements
Exhaustive testing is impossible; stop testing earlier
questions.explanation: Defects found late cost more to fix because more work depends on them. Static testing and early analysis (shift-left) remove them cheaply. The other choices misapply principles.

questions.prompt: A startup building a prototype for investor demos adopts the full documentation and test process of a regulated medical device company. Which principle is being ignored and what is the risk?
options: Testing is context dependent; heavy process wastes time on a short-lived prototype while missing the risks that matter (e.g. demo-critical flows)
Tests wear out; they will repeat tests
Defects cluster together; they will find too many defects
No principle; more process is always better
questions.explanation: The appropriate depth and formality of testing depend on context: risk, domain, lifecycle and constraints. A prototype needs fast, focused testing of what matters for its purpose, not regulated-grade documentation.
